Returning to college

Do my old college credits still count? Start with the courses you already earned

An old course does not become useless simply because time has passed. Its value depends on the school and degree you choose, the original course record, and any subject-specific rules. Begin with a course inventory, then compare what those courses can satisfy in realistic degree options.

You may have more of a starting point than you think

Returning students often remember the time and money they spent but no longer have a clear picture of the work completed. Several colleges, one old exam, a certificate, and an unfinished term can feel like a pile of unrelated records. Bringing them into one collection turns that uncertainty into something you can compare.

The first goal is to record what you actually earned. A completed course, a course you are currently taking, and a course you merely want to take have different statuses. Keep them distinct even when they share a title. A rough “about 60 credits” estimate can help frame a conversation, but it should not be treated as 60 credits already applied to a new degree.

There is no need to type everything one course at a time. DegreeSteps accepts transcript PDFs, spreadsheets, and its labeled CSV template. Review the extracted rows before adding them. The import brings in original learning; it does not manufacture a university award.

Three questions explain most of the uncertainty

First, will the receiving institution accept the original source and record? The school may need an official transcript from each college or an appropriate exam or training transcript. A course copied onto a later transcript can still need documentation from its original issuer.

Second, does the course have an age or recency restriction for this requirement? General electives and tightly sequenced professional subjects may be treated differently. For example, the reviewed WGU Business Management rules identify five-year recency conditions for specific spreadsheet and project-management requirements. That is a program-specific rule, not a claim that all college courses expire after five years.

Third, where can the course be used now? A class that once counted in a major may fit a general-education requirement or elective at another destination. Acceptance is useful only to the extent that the chosen degree still has a place for the credit.

Build a collection that can travel between plans

Keep the original provider or institution, course code and title, credit amount and unit system, completion date, and grade or score when available. A semester credit, quarter credit, and WGU competency unit are not automatically interchangeable. The receiving school’s actual award should be recorded separately.

If you do not have every detail, preserve what you know and return with the record later. Do not guess a missing course code from a similar title or convert an unknown credit amount into an earned total. Keeping the uncertainty attached to the particular row makes the rest of the inventory usable.

A useful inventory keeps original facts separate from new degree placements.
Keep in your course collectionWhy it helps
Original college or providerIdentifies the source the receiving school evaluates
Course code and titleSupports an exact match rather than a title guess
Credits and unit systemKeeps source quantity distinct from receiving awards

Compare what is left, rather than starting over

Imagine two hypothetical 120-credit degrees. Your original records receive proposed placements of 45 credits in one route and 60 in the other. That does not automatically make the second route the better choice. You also need its remaining university coursework, fees, schedule, major requirements, and fit with your career goal.

A degree that uses more existing credit can still require a longer prerequisite sequence. A different route may offer a useful campus experience or the specific academic preparation you need. For a licensed profession, the approved preparation and professional requirements remain part of the decision.

Use the same inventory in each comparison. That makes the differences visible without editing what you earned. When a degree changes, a course can move from a major slot to an elective or stop applying; the original course remains in your collection for another comparison.

Choose new coursework after seeing the gaps

Once your existing learning has been considered, the remaining rows become a much more useful shopping list. You can look for an eligible self-paced course, a credit exam, institutional coursework, or required study at the final university only where it fills a real gap.

This order can prevent paying twice for the same subject. It can also reveal that a broad elective you were about to buy has no open space left in the degree. Provider subscriptions are easier to budget when the basket contains courses that actually help.

An official evaluation remains the institution’s decision. DegreeSteps keeps original records, source-supported proposed matches, and individual school awards separate so you can move forward with a clear view of which is which.

Your next step can be small

Start with the records you have, even if that is one unofficial transcript. Upload it, review the extracted courses, and add any other records when you find them. If you have no transcript ready, a provisional degree plan can still help you understand the destination while the course collection is refined.

The useful question is not whether your previous effort was wasted. It is which degree makes the best use of that effort while leading where you want to go. Seeing that comparison is a practical first step back into higher education.

About this research

DegreeSteps editorial team · Degree planning and transfer-credit research

We explain educational choices using university catalogs, receiving-school course agreements, provider guidance, and the same researched degree models used by DegreeSteps. Our articles distinguish proposed coursework, original learning records, and individual university awards. Worked examples identify their program, format, units, and relevant dates.
